name: Acute Otitis Media
description: Acute otitis media is a bacterial or viral infection of the middle ear space, most common in children under 5. It causes rapid onset ear pain, fever, and temporary hearing difficulty. Without treatment it may perforate the eardrum or spread to the mastoid bone.
diagnosticClues: red bulging tympanic membrane on otoscopy

laboratory: ear swab culture if discharge present

procedural: myringotomy if severe or not resolving
surgical: grommet insertion for recurrent episodes (3 or more in 6 months)

referralThresholdReason: Most resolve with GP treatment. ENT if no improvement in 72 hours, recurrent episodes, or any red flag present.
urgencyRationale: Painful and distressing but rarely immediately life-threatening. Mastoiditis complication is a medical emergency.
patientAdvice: Give regular pain relief and keep the ear dry. If fever worsens, ear starts draining pus, or there is swelling behind the ear, go to the emergency room immediately.

accessConsiderations: often managed by patent medicine vendors without diagnosis
ENT access limited outside Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan

name: Otitis Media with Effusion
description: Otitis media with effusion is a collection of sticky or watery fluid behind an intact eardrum without signs of acute infection. It causes muffled hearing and a blocked feeling in the ear. It often follows a cold or ear infection and usually clears by itself, but can persist for months.

primary: incomplete resolution of acute otitis media

diagnosticClues: fluid level or air bubbles behind drum

imaging: MRI or CT postnasal space if unilateral in adult

selfCare: seat child near front of class

referralThresholdReason: Most cases resolve spontaneously. Refer if persisting beyond 3 months with hearing loss, or earlier if speech or learning is affected.
urgencyRationale: Not dangerous but can affect hearing, speech and schooling if prolonged.
patientAdvice: Most children improve within three months. Seat the child close to the teacher and speak clearly. See a doctor if hearing stays poor beyond three months or speech seems delayed.

accessConsiderations: tympanometry rarely available outside tertiary centres
hearing problems mistaken for inattention at school

name: Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media
description: Chronic suppurative otitis media is a long-standing infection of the middle ear with a hole in the eardrum and persistent or recurring pus discharge. It usually causes painless ear discharge and reduced hearing. It can lead to serious complications if neglected.
diagnosticClues: central perforation with wet or mucoid discharge

imaging: CT temporal bone if complication or cholesteatoma suspected

selfCare: keep ear dry with cotton wool and petroleum jelly when bathing
do not insert objects into ear

referralThresholdReason: Delay risks cholesteatoma, mastoid disease and intracranial complications.
urgencyRationale: Chronic and often not painful, but can progress to dangerous complications.
patientAdvice: Keep the ear dry and do not use herbal or oily drops. See a doctor this week for proper ear drops and assessment. Go to emergency care if you develop swelling behind the ear, facial weakness or severe headache.
preventionTips: treat ear infections early and fully

localFactors: leading cause of preventable hearing loss in children
traditional ear remedies such as herbal drops and urine
accessConsiderations: patent medicine vendors dispense oral antibiotics instead of ear drops

name: Otitis Externa
description: Otitis externa is inflammation or infection of the skin lining the outer ear canal. It causes pain that worsens when the ear is touched or pulled, itching and discharge. It is often triggered by moisture or scratching the canal.

primary: ear pain worse on touching the ear

redFlags: severe pain in a diabetic or immunocompromised person
swelling spreading to face or neck
diagnosticClues: pain on tragal pressure or pinna traction
referralThresholdReason: Responds to drops at GP level. Refer if no improvement in a week, if diabetic with severe pain, or if recurrent.
urgencyRationale: Painful but self-limiting with treatment. Rare spread to skull base in at-risk people is dangerous.
patientAdvice: Keep water out of the ear and do not scratch it. Use prescribed ear drops. See a doctor if pain worsens or you are diabetic.

localFactors: use of cotton buds, matchsticks and hairpins to clean ears

name: Otomycosis
description: Otomycosis is a fungal infection of the outer ear canal, common in hot humid climates. It causes intense itching, fullness and sometimes fluffy debris in the ear. It is often triggered by prolonged antibiotic drop use or moisture.

contributing: prior topical antibiotic or steroid use

redFlags: severe deep ear pain in diabetic
diagnosticClues: white, grey or black fluffy debris like wet newspaper

selfCare: stop self-applied oils and unknown drops

referralThresholdReason: Manageable with cleaning and antifungal drops. Refer if persistent, recurrent or diabetic.
urgencyRationale: Uncomfortable but not dangerous in healthy people.
patientAdvice: Keep the ear dry and avoid putting oils or herbal liquids in it. See a doctor for cleaning and antifungal drops. Check your blood sugar if diabetic.
preventionTips: avoid long courses of antibiotic drops
do not clean ears with sticks

localFactors: hot humid climate favours fungal growth
unregulated antibiotic drops sold over the counter
accessConsiderations: antifungal ear preparations not always stocked

name: Malignant (Necrotising) Otitis Externa
description: Malignant otitis externa is an aggressive infection spreading from the ear canal into the bone at the base of the skull. It mostly affects elderly diabetics and immunocompromised people. It causes severe deep ear pain and can paralyse cranial nerves.

primary: severe deep ear pain worse at night

redFlags: severe unremitting ear pain in diabetic
diagnosticClues: granulation tissue at canal floor junction
failure of usual otitis externa treatment
referralThresholdReason: Delay allows skull base osteomyelitis and cranial nerve palsies with high mortality.
urgencyRationale: Life-threatening in diabetics if missed, requiring prolonged hospital-based treatment.
patientAdvice: Severe ear pain in a diabetic or immunocompromised person that is not improving needs a doctor within 24 hours. Go to hospital immediately if the face droops or swallowing becomes difficult.

name: Tinnitus
description: Tinnitus is the perception of ringing, buzzing, hissing or other sound in the ear or head without an external source. It is a symptom rather than a disease and has many causes. It may be constant or intermittent and can disturb sleep and concentration.

rare: pulsating sound in time with heartbeat

contributing: ototoxic medicines such as aminoglycosides, quinine and high-dose aspirin

redFlags: tinnitus with facial weakness or neurological signs
diagnosticClues: associated high frequency hearing loss on audiogram

imaging: MRI internal auditory meatus for unilateral or pulsatile tinnitus

surgical: rarely for vascular or structural causes

referralThresholdReason: Most tinnitus is benign. Urgent referral for one-sided, pulsatile, sudden or neurologically associated tinnitus.
urgencyRationale: Usually benign but distressing. Unilateral or pulsatile forms may signal serious pathology.
patientAdvice: Protect your ears from loud noise and use background sound at night. See a doctor if the ringing is only in one ear, pulses with your heartbeat, or comes with sudden hearing loss.
preventionTips: wear ear protection around loud noise

localFactors: noise from generators, markets and religious events
quinine and chloroquine use for malaria
accessConsiderations: audiology services limited to major cities
no tinnitus therapy services in most areas

name: Conductive Hearing Loss
description: Conductive hearing loss occurs when sound cannot pass efficiently through the outer or middle ear. Causes include wax, fluid, perforation or bone problems. Many causes are treatable and hearing can often be restored.
redFlags: hearing loss after head injury with bleeding or clear fluid from ear

imaging: CT temporal bone if structural cause suspected

selfCare: protect ear from water if perforated

referralThresholdReason: Usually treatable. Refer for audiometry and diagnosis if not due to simple wax or resolving infection.
urgencyRationale: Rarely dangerous but impacts communication, schooling and work.
patientAdvice: Do not poke your ears. See a doctor to find the cause, as many causes of this type of hearing loss are easily treated.

localFactors: chronic ear infections and untreated otitis media
accessConsiderations: audiologist access limited in rural areas

name: Sensorineural Hearing Loss
description: Sensorineural hearing loss results from damage to the inner ear or hearing nerve. Sound is heard but unclear, especially in noisy places. It is usually permanent, though sudden onset cases need urgent treatment.
redFlags: sudden hearing loss over hours to 3 days

imaging: MRI internal auditory canals for asymmetric loss

selfCare: face speaker and reduce background noise

referralThresholdReason: Chronic cases routine. Sudden onset is urgent as treatment works best within days.
urgencyRationale: Usually permanent and non-dangerous, but sudden or asymmetric loss needs prompt assessment.
patientAdvice: Get your hearing tested. If hearing dropped suddenly in one ear, see a doctor within 24 hours. Hearing aids can help many people.
preventionTips: vaccinate against measles, mumps and meningitis

localFactors: Lassa fever related deafness in endemic areas

name: Mixed Hearing Loss
description: Mixed hearing loss combines a conductive component from the outer or middle ear with a sensorineural component from the inner ear or nerve. It is common in long-standing ear disease and elderly people. Treatment targets the treatable conductive part and supports the rest with amplification.

primary: hearing loss in one or both ears
chronic otitis media with inner ear damage

diagnosticClues: air-bone gap with raised bone conduction thresholds
referralThresholdReason: Needs audiological and ENT assessment to separate treatable components.
urgencyRationale: Not dangerous but significantly affects daily communication.
patientAdvice: See an ENT clinic for hearing tests. Part of the loss may be treatable, and hearing aids can help with the rest.

accessConsiderations: audiology services scarce outside major cities

name: Cholesteatoma
commonName: Skin cyst in the middle ear
description: Cholesteatoma is an abnormal collection of skin cells in the middle ear that grows and erodes surrounding bone. It causes foul-smelling ear discharge and hearing loss. It does not resolve with antibiotics and requires surgery.
diagnosticClues: attic retraction pocket with keratin debris

surgical: canal wall up or down techniques

referralThresholdReason: Progressive bone erosion can damage hearing, balance, facial nerve and cause intracranial infection.
urgencyRationale: Destructive growth with serious complication risk, but typically slow.
patientAdvice: Persistent smelly ear discharge that does not clear with drops needs ENT review this week. Seek emergency care if you have facial weakness, severe vertigo or severe headache.

accessConsiderations: CT scanning and mastoid surgery available mainly in tertiary hospitals

name: Meniere's Disease
description: Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder causing episodes of vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, ringing and ear fullness. Attacks last from 20 minutes to several hours. It is thought to involve excess fluid pressure in the inner ear.

primary: episodic vertigo lasting 20 minutes to hours

diagnosticClues: low frequency sensorineural loss on audiogram
episodes of vertigo with ear fullness and tinnitus

imaging: MRI internal auditory canals to exclude acoustic neuroma

referralThresholdReason: Chronic relapsing condition needing diagnosis and long-term plan. Urgent if sudden hearing loss or neurological features.
urgencyRationale: Disabling episodes but not life-threatening.
patientAdvice: During an attack sit or lie still and take prescribed anti-sickness tablets. Reduce salt and caffeine. Do not drive when dizzy. Seek urgent care if you have weakness, speech difficulty or severe headache.

localFactors: high-salt diets and bouillon cube use
vertigo often self-treated as malaria or hypertension

name: Labyrinthitis
description: Labyrinthitis is inflammation of the inner ear, usually after a viral illness, affecting both balance and hearing. It causes sudden severe vertigo with hearing loss and ringing. Most people recover over weeks, though hearing may not fully return.

imaging: MRI brain and IAM if central cause suspected

surgical: mastoidectomy if bacterial from middle ear

referralThresholdReason: Sudden vertigo with hearing loss needs prompt exclusion of stroke and early treatment to protect hearing.
urgencyRationale: Severe symptoms and need to exclude central causes; hearing recovery depends on early care.
patientAdvice: Rest and avoid sudden movements. Do not drive. See a doctor within 24 hours. Go to emergency care if you have severe headache, weakness, trouble speaking or double vision.
preventionTips: vaccination against measles, mumps and meningitis

localFactors: vertigo often mistaken for malaria or high blood pressure

name: Vestibular Neuritis
description: Vestibular neuritis is inflammation of the balance nerve, usually after a viral infection. It causes sudden prolonged vertigo and unsteadiness without hearing loss. Symptoms improve over days to weeks as the brain compensates.

selfCare: rest briefly then gradually resume activity
medication: short course antiemetics or vestibular suppressants (no more than 3 days)

referralThresholdReason: Central causes like stroke can mimic this and must be excluded promptly.
urgencyRationale: Very distressing but self-limiting; exclusion of stroke is time-critical.
patientAdvice: Rest for a day or two, then start moving gently as this helps recovery. Seek emergency help for weakness, speech difficulty, severe headache or double vision.
keywords: dizzy and vomiting no hearing loss

localFactors: dizziness commonly attributed to malaria or hypertension
accessConsiderations: stroke mimics need CT or MRI

name: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo
description: BPPV is the most common cause of vertigo, caused by displaced crystals in the inner ear canals. Brief spinning episodes are triggered by head position changes such as rolling over in bed. It is harmless and can usually be cured with simple manoeuvres.

primary: brief spinning triggered by head movement

typicalDuration: episodes of seconds to a minute; weeks to months
diagnosticClues: positive Dix-Hallpike test with torsional nystagmus

selfCare: Epley manoeuvre at home when taught

referralThresholdReason: Easily diagnosed and treated at GP level. Refer if atypical, persistent or recurrent.
urgencyRationale: Harmless but affects daily life and increases fall risk.
patientAdvice: Move slowly when changing position, and see a doctor who can perform a repositioning manoeuvre, which usually cures it. Seek emergency care if dizziness comes with weakness or speech problems.
keywords: room spins when I look up

localFactors: dizziness often blamed on blood pressure or malaria and treated with drugs
accessConsiderations: Epley manoeuvre not widely known to GPs

name: Ear Barotrauma
description: Ear barotrauma is injury to the ear from rapid pressure changes, such as flying or diving, when the Eustachian tube fails to equalise pressure. It causes ear pain, fullness and muffled hearing. Most cases settle in days, though severe cases can rupture the eardrum.

primary: ear pain during or after flying or diving
pressure differences between middle ear and environment

referralThresholdReason: Usually self-limiting. Refer for persistent symptoms, vertigo or hearing loss.
urgencyRationale: Usually benign; inner ear barotrauma is the exception.
patientAdvice: Swallow or chew during take-off and landing. Avoid flying or diving with a blocked nose. See a doctor if hearing loss or dizziness follows.
preventionTips: do not dive with a blocked nose

name: Earwax Impaction
description: Earwax impaction occurs when wax builds up and blocks the ear canal. It causes a blocked feeling and reduced hearing. It is common and easily treated, but cleaning with objects often makes it worse.
diagnosticClues: wax visible occluding canal on otoscopy
conductive hearing loss that improves after removal

specialist: audiometry if hearing does not improve

selfCare: olive oil or wax-softening drops for 5-7 days

referralThresholdReason: Easily treated at GP or nurse level.
urgencyRationale: Harmless but troublesome.
patientAdvice: Do not use cotton buds or sharp objects. Use softening drops for a week and see a nurse or doctor for removal if still blocked.
preventionTips: periodic review if hearing aid user

localFactors: use of cotton buds, matchsticks, hairpins and local objects
accessConsiderations: syringing sometimes done by untrained persons

name: Tympanic Membrane Perforation
description: A perforated eardrum is a hole in the thin membrane separating the ear canal from the middle ear. It can follow infection, pressure injury, trauma or a slap to the ear. Many small perforations heal on their own.

primary: sudden ear pain that then eases

redFlags: clear fluid leak after head injury

selfCare: keep ear dry using cotton wool with petroleum jelly
surgical: myringoplasty or tympanoplasty if not healing

referralThresholdReason: Most heal spontaneously but trauma-related or persistent perforations need ENT assessment.
urgencyRationale: Typically heals; risks are infection and hearing loss.
patientAdvice: Keep the ear dry and do not put anything in it. See a doctor this week, especially if hearing loss, dizziness or discharge persists.

localFactors: slaps to the ear as discipline or assault

name: Acute Mastoiditis
commonName: Infection of the bone behind the ear
description: Acute mastoiditis is infection of the mastoid bone behind the ear, usually spreading from acute otitis media. It causes pain, redness and swelling behind the ear and pushes the ear forward. It is a medical emergency because it can spread to the brain.

primary: swelling and redness behind the ear

referralThresholdReason: Risk of meningitis, brain abscess, sinus thrombosis and facial nerve damage.
urgencyRationale: Potentially life-threatening intracranial spread requiring hospital treatment.
patientAdvice: Go to the emergency department now if there is swelling or redness behind the ear with fever or ear pain.
preventionTips: complete antibiotic courses for ear infections

localFactors: untreated or partially treated otitis media

name: Vestibular Schwannoma
description: Acoustic neuroma is a slow-growing, non-cancerous tumour on the balance and hearing nerve. It usually causes gradual one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. Large tumours can press on the brainstem.

primary: gradual hearing loss in one ear
Schwann cell tumour of the vestibular nerve

diagnosticClues: MRI enhancing mass in cerebellopontine angle

imaging: MRI internal auditory canals with gadolinium

referralThresholdReason: Needs MRI and specialist review; growth can compress brainstem if neglected.
urgencyRationale: Benign and slow-growing but can become dangerous when large.
patientAdvice: One-sided hearing loss or ringing should be checked with a hearing test and MRI. Book an ENT appointment this week.

accessConsiderations: neurosurgery and radiosurgery limited to few centres

name: Otosclerosis
description: Otosclerosis is abnormal bone growth that fixes the stapes bone in the middle ear, causing progressive conductive hearing loss. It often starts in young adults and runs in families. It is treatable with surgery or hearing aids.

primary: abnormal bone remodelling around stapes footplate

referralThresholdReason: Slowly progressive; surgery and hearing aids can restore hearing.
urgencyRationale: Not dangerous; quality of life impacted.
patientAdvice: Slowly worsening hearing with a normal-looking ear should be assessed by an ENT specialist. Surgery or hearing aids can help.
preventionTips: early hearing assessment if family history

localFactors: less common in Black African populations
accessConsiderations: stapes surgery limited to few specialist centres

name: Presbycusis
description: Presbycusis is the gradual, symmetrical loss of hearing that comes with ageing, mainly affecting high-pitched sounds. Speech becomes hard to follow, especially in noisy places. It is very common and helped by hearing aids.

primary: gradual hearing loss in both ears
degeneration of cochlear hair cells and nerve fibres

redFlags: hearing loss with vertigo or facial weakness
diagnosticClues: symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural loss on audiogram
referralThresholdReason: Slow, benign progression; hearing assessment improves quality of life.
urgencyRationale: Not dangerous but strongly linked to isolation and cognitive decline.
patientAdvice: Get your hearing tested and consider hearing aids. See a doctor urgently if hearing loss is sudden or only in one ear.

localFactors: hearing loss often accepted as normal ageing
accessConsiderations: hearing aids costly and rarely subsidised

name: Auricular Perichondritis
description: Perichondritis is infection of the tissue covering the ear cartilage, often after piercing, trauma or surgery. The outer ear becomes red, swollen and very painful, sparing the earlobe. Without prompt treatment cartilage can die and the ear may become deformed.
referralThresholdReason: Cartilage destruction and cauliflower ear can occur within days.
urgencyRationale: Rapidly progressive infection with permanent deformity risk.
patientAdvice: Remove any ear jewellery and see a doctor within a day for antibiotics. Do not squeeze or burst the swelling.

name: Ear Canal Foreign Body
description: An ear canal foreign body is an object or insect lodged in the ear. It is most common in children, who push beads, seeds or small toys into the ear. Attempts to remove it at home can push it deeper and damage the eardrum.

primary: feeling of something in the ear

selfCare: for insect: tilt head and add oil to drown it
procedural: removal with hooks, forceps or suction
surgical: general anaesthetic removal in uncooperative children

referralThresholdReason: Delay increases risk of canal and eardrum injury; batteries and seeds are urgent.
urgencyRationale: Usually not dangerous but button batteries and failed removal attempts need urgent care.
patientAdvice: Do not try to remove it yourself and do not flush with water if it is a seed or bean. See a doctor within a day. Go to emergency care at once if it is a button battery.
preventionTips: keep small objects away from young children

localFactors: children inserting seeds, beads and pencil parts

name: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss
description: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is rapid hearing loss in one ear occurring over hours to three days. The cause is often unknown. It is an ENT emergency because early steroid treatment improves the chance of recovery.

primary: sudden hearing loss in one ear

diagnosticClues: sensorineural loss of 30 dB or more across 3 frequencies within 72 hours
referralThresholdReason: Steroids are most effective within 72 hours and benefit declines after two weeks.
urgencyRationale: Time-critical for hearing preservation.
patientAdvice: If your hearing dropped suddenly in one ear, see a doctor the same day. Do not wait to see if it improves, as early treatment matters.
preventionTips: control blood pressure, diabetes and cholesterol
keywords: woke up deaf in one ear

localFactors: often dismissed as wax or catarrh

name: Noise-Induced Hearing Loss
description: Noise-induced hearing loss is permanent damage to inner ear hair cells from loud sound. It develops gradually with repeated exposure or suddenly after a blast. It often starts with ringing and trouble hearing high-pitched sounds.

primary: repeated loud noise exposure above 85 dB

diagnosticClues: bilateral high-frequency notch at 4 kHz on audiogram
referralThresholdReason: Permanent but preventable; early audiometry guides protection.
urgencyRationale: Irreversible but slowly progressive; acute blast injury is more urgent.
patientAdvice: Wear earplugs or earmuffs around loud noise and keep headphone volume low. Get a hearing test if you notice ringing or muffled hearing.
preventionTips: keep distance from loudspeakers and generators

name: Ramsay Hunt Syndrome
commonName: Shingles of the ear with facial paralysis
description: Ramsay Hunt syndrome occurs when the shingles virus affects the facial nerve near the ear. It causes a painful blistering rash in or around the ear, facial weakness and sometimes hearing loss or vertigo. Early antiviral and steroid treatment improves recovery.

primary: painful blisters in or around the ear
rare: dry eye with inability to close eyelid

diagnosticClues: vesicles in ear canal or concha
referralThresholdReason: Antivirals and steroids work best within 72 hours of onset.
urgencyRationale: Treatment time-sensitive; poor recovery of facial nerve if delayed.
patientAdvice: See a doctor within 24 hours if you have an ear rash with facial weakness. Protect your eye and use lubricating drops.

accessConsiderations: often misdiagnosed as stroke or spiritual attack

name: Auricular Haematoma
description: Auricular haematoma is a collection of blood between the ear cartilage and its covering skin after a blow. It causes a swollen, bruised and tense outer ear. If not drained quickly it can cause permanent cauliflower deformity.

primary: blunt trauma or shearing force to the pinna

diagnosticClues: smooth tense swelling of anterior pinna

procedural: needle aspiration or incision and drainage with pressure dressing

referralThresholdReason: Delayed drainage causes cartilage damage and permanent deformity.
urgencyRationale: Time-sensitive for cosmetic and infective complications.
patientAdvice: Apply a cold pack and see a doctor within 24 hours for drainage and a pressure dressing.
preventionTips: seek care early after ear injury

name: Allergic Rhinitis
description: Allergic rhinitis is inflammation of the nose caused by an allergic reaction to dust, pollen, moulds or animal dander. It causes sneezing, runny and blocked nose and itchy eyes. It can be seasonal or year-round and often coexists with asthma.
referralThresholdReason: Well managed in primary care. Refer if refractory, complicated by polyps or sinusitis, or asthma is uncontrolled.
urgencyRationale: Chronic and bothersome but not dangerous.
patientAdvice: Avoid dust and triggers, rinse your nose with salt water and use a steroid nasal spray daily. See a doctor if symptoms persist or you have wheeze.
preventionTips: keep windows closed on dusty days

accessConsiderations: patent medicine vendors sell antihistamines and unproven decongestants
intranasal steroids costly and not always available

name: Non-Allergic Rhinitis
description: Non-allergic rhinitis causes nasal congestion, runny nose or postnasal drip without an allergic cause. Triggers include irritants, weather changes, strong smells and hormonal changes. Tests for allergy are negative.

primary: irritants such as smoke and fumes

imaging: CT sinuses if sinus disease suspected

referralThresholdReason: Managed in primary care; refer for refractory symptoms or abnormal findings.
urgencyRationale: Benign, chronic, quality-of-life condition.
patientAdvice: Avoid smoke and strong fumes, use salt water nasal rinses and see your doctor for a nasal spray if symptoms persist.

accessConsiderations: often managed with oral decongestants from vendors

name: Rhinitis Medicamentosa
description: Rhinitis medicamentosa is rebound nasal congestion caused by using decongestant nasal drops or sprays for more than a few days. The nose becomes blocked whenever the spray wears off, leading to dependence. Stopping the spray and using steroid sprays resolves it.
typicalDuration: weeks to months until spray stopped
diagnosticClues: history of nasal drops use beyond 5-7 days

imaging: CT only if sinus disease suspected

medication: short course oral steroid in severe cases

referralThresholdReason: Responds to stopping spray with steroid spray; refer if refractory.
urgencyRationale: Not dangerous but persists until the spray is stopped.
patientAdvice: Do not use decongestant nasal drops for more than five days. Stop gradually and use salt-water rinses and a steroid spray as advised by your doctor.
keywords: nose blocked after spray wears off

localFactors: decongestant drops freely sold in pharmacies and kiosks

name: Acute Sinusitis
description: Acute sinusitis is inflammation of the sinus linings, usually after a viral cold, lasting less than four weeks. It causes facial pressure, blocked nose and thick discharge. Most cases are viral and settle without antibiotics.
redFlags: swelling or redness around the eye

medication: antibiotics if severe or persisting beyond 10 days

referralThresholdReason: Most resolve at GP level; refer for complications, recurrence or no response.
urgencyRationale: Usually self-limiting but orbital or intracranial spread is dangerous.
patientAdvice: Use salt-water rinses, rest and pain relief. See a doctor if symptoms last over 10 days or worsen. Go to emergency care for eye swelling, double vision or severe headache.

name: Chronic Rhinosinusitis
description: Chronic rhinosinusitis is sinus and nasal inflammation lasting 12 weeks or more. It causes blocked nose, discharge, facial pressure and reduced smell. It may occur with or without nasal polyps.
diagnosticClues: purulent discharge or polyps on endoscopy
referralThresholdReason: Needs endoscopic assessment and CT if medical therapy fails.
urgencyRationale: Quality-of-life condition; complications are rare.
patientAdvice: Use daily salt-water rinses and your steroid spray. Book an ENT visit if symptoms continue beyond three months.

accessConsiderations: FESS only at tertiary and some private centres

name: Fungal Sinusitis
description: Fungal sinusitis ranges from fungal balls and allergic fungal sinusitis to aggressive invasive disease. It causes persistent blockage, thick discharge and facial pain. Invasive fungal sinusitis in diabetics or immunosuppressed patients is life-threatening.
typicalDuration: weeks to months; invasive form progresses within days
redFlags: black necrotic tissue in nose or palate
fever in a diabetic or immunosuppressed person
diagnosticClues: fungal debris or allergic mucin on endoscopy

imaging: MRI if orbital or intracranial extension

referralThresholdReason: Invasive forms progress rapidly and can cause blindness and death.
urgencyRationale: Invasive disease is life-threatening; non-invasive forms are chronic and troublesome.
patientAdvice: Persistent one-sided sinus symptoms, especially in a diabetic, need prompt ENT review. Go to emergency care for black discharge, eye swelling or vision changes.
preventionTips: avoid long steroid courses without supervision

name: Nasal Polyps
description: Nasal polyps are soft, painless, grape-like swellings of the nasal and sinus lining. They cause blocked nose, loss of smell and runny nose. They are linked to chronic inflammation, asthma and aspirin sensitivity.
diagnosticClues: pale, translucent, mobile masses on endoscopy
referralThresholdReason: Needs endoscopy; urgent if one-sided, bleeding or atypical.
urgencyRationale: Benign but recurrent; unilateral polyps may hide tumour.
patientAdvice: Use your steroid nasal spray regularly and rinse with salt water. See an ENT doctor, and more urgently if the nose is blocked on one side only or bleeds.

accessConsiderations: polypectomy available in tertiary and private clinics

name: Deviated Nasal Septum
description: A deviated septum is when the wall between the nostrils is displaced to one side, narrowing an airway. It may be present from birth or follow injury. Many people have no symptoms, but some have blocked nose, nosebleeds or sinus problems.

imaging: CT sinuses if sinus disease suspected

referralThresholdReason: Surgery is elective and only needed when symptoms persist.
urgencyRationale: Structural and benign.
patientAdvice: If your nose is persistently blocked on one side, book an ENT appointment. Medical treatment helps first; surgery is considered if it fails.

localFactors: trauma from fights and road traffic accidents
accessConsiderations: septoplasty at tertiary and private centres

name: Nasal Fracture
description: A nasal fracture is a break in the nasal bones or cartilage after injury. It causes swelling, bruising, pain and sometimes deformity and nosebleed. Early assessment prevents septal haematoma and permanent obstruction.
referralThresholdReason: Reduction ideally within 5-10 days before bones set; septal haematoma needs same-day drainage.
urgencyRationale: Time-limited window for reduction; haematoma and CSF leak are urgent.
patientAdvice: Apply ice, keep your head raised and avoid blowing your nose. See a doctor within a week for assessment. Seek emergency help for clear fluid leaking from the nose or vision changes.

name: Septal Haematoma
description: A septal haematoma is a collection of blood between the septal cartilage and its lining after nasal injury. It causes bilateral nasal blockage and a bulging septum. It needs urgent drainage to prevent cartilage death and nose collapse.

primary: both nostrils blocked after nasal injury

typicalDuration: needs drainage within hours to days

procedural: incision and drainage with nasal packing

referralThresholdReason: Untreated haematoma becomes abscess and destroys septal cartilage within days.
urgencyRationale: Rapid cartilage damage and spread of infection risk.
patientAdvice: If both nostrils are blocked after a nose injury, see a doctor today. Drainage must be done quickly to save the nose structure.
keywords: both sides of nose blocked after injury

name: Epistaxis
description: Epistaxis is bleeding from the nose, most commonly from fragile vessels in the front of the septum. It is usually harmless and stops with pressure. Heavy, recurrent or posterior bleeds can be serious.

selfCare: sit forward and pinch soft part of nose for 10-15 minutes

referralThresholdReason: Most stop with first aid; persistent or heavy bleeding needs emergency packing.
urgencyRationale: Usually minor but can cause significant blood loss, especially in the elderly or anticoagulated.
patientAdvice: Sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of your nose firmly for 15 minutes. Go to emergency care if bleeding continues beyond 20 minutes, is heavy, or follows a head injury.

name: Anosmia
description: Anosmia is complete loss of the sense of smell, which also reduces taste. Causes include viral infections, nasal blockage, head injury and neurological disease. Many post-viral cases recover over weeks to months.

secondary: inability to detect smoke or gas

redFlags: loss after head injury with clear nasal fluid

selfCare: smell training with four essential scents twice daily
gas and smoke alarms at home

referralThresholdReason: Many recover; persistent loss needs endoscopy and imaging.
urgencyRationale: Safety risk (gas, smoke, spoiled food); rarely signals serious neurological disease.
patientAdvice: Fit smoke detectors, check food expiry dates and try daily smell training. See an ENT doctor if smell has not returned in 3 months or if loss follows a head injury.

name: Hyposmia
description: Hyposmia is a reduced ability to smell. It is common with colds, allergies and sinus disease and increases with age. It may also be an early sign of neurological conditions.
diagnosticClues: inflamed mucosa or polyps on endoscopy
referralThresholdReason: Usually reversible if due to nasal disease; persistent unexplained loss needs assessment.
urgencyRationale: Quality-of-life and safety issue, rarely dangerous.
patientAdvice: Treat nasal blockage, avoid smoking and try daily smell training. See a doctor if smell does not recover or one side is affected.

accessConsiderations: unsupervised steroid or herbal nasal use

name: Nasal Foreign Body
description: A nasal foreign body is an object pushed into the nose, most often by young children. It can cause one-sided foul-smelling discharge and blockage. Button batteries and magnets are emergencies.

imaging: X-ray for radio-opaque objects if unseen

selfCare: encourage nose blowing on free side
procedural: removal with hook, forceps or suction

referralThresholdReason: Risk of aspiration and tissue damage; batteries cause injury within hours.
urgencyRationale: Usually not life-threatening but aspiration risk and battery injuries are serious.
patientAdvice: Do not use tweezers or try to dig it out. See a doctor today. Go to emergency care at once if you suspect a button battery or the child is struggling to breathe.
preventionTips: keep small objects away from toddlers

name: Adenoid Hypertrophy
description: Adenoid hypertrophy is enlargement of the lymphoid tissue at the back of the nose, mostly in children. It blocks nasal breathing and Eustachian tubes, causing mouth breathing, snoring and ear problems. Many shrink as the child grows.

primary: recurrent infection and inflammation of adenoids

diagnosticClues: enlarged adenoids on endoscopy or lateral X-ray
referralThresholdReason: Surgery considered if persistent obstruction, recurrent otitis or sleep apnoea.
urgencyRationale: Benign; sleep apnoea or hearing problems raise priority.
patientAdvice: If your child snores, breathes through the mouth or has recurrent ear infections, see an ENT clinic. Watch for pauses in breathing at night.

accessConsiderations: adenoidectomy mainly in teaching hospitals and private centres

name: Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
commonName: Cancer at the back of the nose
description: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a cancer arising in the upper throat behind the nose. It often presents with a painless neck lump, blocked nose, nosebleeds or ear fullness. It is linked to Epstein-Barr virus and responds well to radiotherapy if found early.

primary: EBV-associated malignant transformation of nasopharyngeal epithelium

redFlags: unilateral serous otitis media in adult
referralThresholdReason: Early staging significantly improves survival; late presentation is common.
urgencyRationale: Malignant; early treatment is highly effective while advanced disease is life-threatening.
patientAdvice: A painless neck lump or one-sided blocked ear and nose that persists beyond 3 weeks needs urgent specialist assessment. Do not wait.

name: Choanal Atresia
commonName: Blocked back of nose in newborn
description: Choanal atresia is a congenital blockage of the back of the nasal passage by bone or tissue. Newborns breathe through the nose, so bilateral blockage causes breathing difficulty that improves with crying. Unilateral cases may present later with one-sided discharge.

primary: failure of nasal-pharyngeal membrane to open in embryo

diagnosticClues: inability to pass catheter into nasopharynx
referralThresholdReason: Bilateral atresia can cause fatal airway obstruction in newborns.
urgencyRationale: Bilateral form is an airway emergency; unilateral is less urgent.
patientAdvice: A newborn who turns blue while feeding but pinks up when crying needs emergency care immediately.

localFactors: late recognition of newborn airway problems

name: Atrophic Rhinitis
commonName: Dry crusty nose with foul smell
description: Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic nasal condition where the lining thins and nasal passages become abnormally wide and crusted. It causes foul-smelling crusts, a feeling of blockage and loss of smell. Patients often do not smell their own odour.
diagnosticClues: wide nasal cavities with dry green crusts

surgical: nasal cavity narrowing (Young's operation) in severe cases

referralThresholdReason: Chronic condition requiring long-term care.
urgencyRationale: Socially distressing but non-urgent.
patientAdvice: Rinse your nose with salt water daily and use prescribed ointment. See an ENT doctor if crusting and smell persist.

name: Orbital Cellulitis (Sinogenic)
description: Orbital cellulitis is infection of the tissues around and behind the eye, usually spreading from the ethmoid sinuses. It causes swollen red eyelids, painful eye movement and fever. It is an emergency because it can cause blindness and brain infection.

primary: spread of ethmoid sinusitis through thin bone

diagnosticClues: CT showing sinus opacification and orbital collection

imaging: CT orbits and sinuses with contrast

surgical: endoscopic sinus surgery and orbital decompression

referralThresholdReason: Risk of permanent blindness, cavernous sinus thrombosis and brain abscess within hours to days.
urgencyRationale: Sight- and life-threatening.
patientAdvice: Go to the emergency department immediately if the eyelids are swollen with fever, eye pain on movement, double vision or blurred vision.

localFactors: delayed treatment of sinus and dental infection
accessConsiderations: few paediatric ENT or eye specialists

name: Sinonasal Tumour
commonName: Growth in the nose or sinuses
description: Sinonasal tumours are benign or malignant growths in the nasal cavity and sinuses, including inverted papilloma and squamous carcinoma. They typically cause one-sided blockage, bloody discharge and facial changes. Early signs mimic sinusitis, causing delayed diagnosis.
referralThresholdReason: Unilateral nasal symptoms need endoscopy within 2 weeks to exclude malignancy.
urgencyRationale: Possible malignancy with local invasion; delay worsens outcomes.
patientAdvice: A blocked nose on one side with blood-stained discharge that does not clear needs specialist review within a week. Do not treat it as ordinary catarrh.

localFactors: wood dust exposure in carpentry and sawmills

name: Acute Pharyngitis
description: Acute pharyngitis is inflammation of the throat, most often caused by viruses and occasionally by group A streptococcus. It causes sore throat, pain on swallowing and sometimes fever. Most cases settle within a week.
redFlags: drooling or inability to swallow saliva

medication: penicillin if strep confirmed or likely

referralThresholdReason: Most are self-limiting. Refer if red flags or recurrent severe episodes.
urgencyRationale: Mild illness, but rare complications such as abscess need attention.
patientAdvice: Drink plenty of fluids and use simple pain relief. See a doctor if throat pain is severe, lasts over a week or you struggle to swallow or breathe.

accessConsiderations: rheumatic heart disease burden from untreated strep

name: Acute Tonsillitis
description: Acute tonsillitis is infection of the tonsils by viruses or bacteria, causing swollen red tonsils, sore throat and fever. It is common in children and young adults. Bacterial cases may need antibiotics.

medication: penicillin V for 10 days if bacterial
surgical: tonsillectomy for recurrent episodes (7 in 1 year, 5 per year for 2 years, or 3 per year for 3 years)

referralThresholdReason: Typically managed in primary care; refer for recurrent episodes or complications.
urgencyRationale: Painful and may lead to abscess or rheumatic complications if untreated.
patientAdvice: Rest, drink fluids and take pain relief. See a doctor to decide on antibiotics. Seek emergency care if you cannot swallow saliva or breathe comfortably.

name: Chronic Tonsillitis
description: Chronic tonsillitis is persistent or repeated tonsil inflammation with ongoing sore throat, bad breath and tender neck glands. The tonsils may harbour debris and bacteria. Tonsillectomy is considered when episodes are frequent or disabling.
referralThresholdReason: Surgical decision based on frequency and severity; asymmetric tonsil needs urgent assessment.
urgencyRationale: Non-urgent unless suspicion of malignancy.
patientAdvice: Keep a record of your throat infections and see an ENT doctor to discuss whether tonsil removal helps. Report any one-sided tonsil swelling quickly.

accessConsiderations: tonsillectomy available mainly in tertiary and private centres

name: Peritonsillar Abscess
description: A peritonsillar abscess is a pus collection between the tonsil and the throat wall, usually after tonsillitis. It causes severe one-sided throat pain, difficulty opening the mouth and a muffled voice. It needs drainage and antibiotics.

imaging: CT neck with contrast if unclear

referralThresholdReason: Needs drainage; risk of airway obstruction and deep neck spread.
urgencyRationale: Potential airway compromise and deep neck infection.
patientAdvice: If one side of your throat is severely painful and you cannot open your mouth, go to hospital today. Do not delay.

accessConsiderations: drainage requires ENT or trained doctor

name: Acute Laryngitis
description: Acute laryngitis is inflammation of the voice box, usually from a viral infection or voice overuse. It causes hoarseness or loss of voice. Most cases resolve within two weeks with voice rest.
diagnosticClues: red swollen vocal cords on laryngoscopy
referralThresholdReason: Self-limiting; hoarseness beyond 3 weeks requires laryngoscopy to exclude cancer.
urgencyRationale: Benign when short; persistent hoarseness needs exclusion of cancer.
patientAdvice: Rest your voice, drink fluids and avoid smoking. See a doctor if hoarseness lasts more than three weeks or you have breathing difficulty.

localFactors: heavy voice use among preachers, teachers and traders

name: Acute Epiglottitis
description: Epiglottitis is a rapidly progressive infection and swelling of the epiglottis that can block the airway. It causes severe sore throat, muffled voice and drooling. It is a life-threatening emergency in both children and adults.
diagnosticClues: thumb sign on lateral neck X-ray

clinical: observation only; avoid examining throat in child

selfCare: none; do not lie patient flat

referralThresholdReason: Airway can close within hours.
urgencyRationale: Rapid airway obstruction and death risk.
patientAdvice: Call emergency services immediately. Keep the person calm and sitting upright. Do not examine the throat or lay them flat.
preventionTips: prompt care for severe sore throat
keywords: child sitting forward struggling to breathe

name: Croup
description: Croup is a viral infection of the voice box and windpipe in young children causing a barking cough, hoarse voice and noisy breathing. It is worse at night. Most cases are mild, but severe cases can obstruct breathing.
referralThresholdReason: Mild cases treated at home; stridor at rest needs hospital.
urgencyRationale: Usually mild but risk of airway obstruction in young children.
patientAdvice: Keep the child calm and upright. Go to emergency care if noisy breathing continues at rest, the child is struggling, or lips look blue.

name: Vocal Cord Nodules
description: Vocal cord nodules are small, callus-like growths on both vocal cords caused by repeated voice misuse. They produce a breathy, hoarse voice. They are common in teachers, singers and preachers, and respond to voice therapy.
diagnosticClues: bilateral symmetrical nodules at junction of anterior and middle thirds
referralThresholdReason: Voice therapy first line; hoarseness over 3 weeks needs laryngoscopy.
urgencyRationale: Benign; affects occupational voice use.
patientAdvice: Rest your voice and avoid shouting or whispering. Stay hydrated and see an ENT doctor for a laryngeal examination if hoarseness persists.

localFactors: heavy voice use by teachers, preachers, market traders and hawkers

name: Vocal Cord Polyps
description: Vocal cord polyps are soft, usually one-sided swellings on a vocal cord, often after vocal strain, smoking or reflux. They cause hoarseness and a breathy voice. Surgery is often needed when voice therapy fails.

primary: vocal fold trauma and vascular injury

diagnosticClues: unilateral soft sessile or pedunculated lesion on vocal cord
referralThresholdReason: Persistent hoarseness requires laryngoscopy to exclude malignancy.
urgencyRationale: Usually benign, but similar to early cancer in smokers.
patientAdvice: Stop smoking, rest your voice and see an ENT doctor for a throat camera examination if hoarseness persists over three weeks.

localFactors: vocal strain in preaching and trading
accessConsiderations: microlaryngeal surgery limited to tertiary centres

name: Vocal Cord Paralysis
description: Vocal cord paralysis occurs when one or both vocal cords cannot move due to nerve injury. It causes a weak breathy voice, choking on liquids and sometimes breathing difficulty. Common causes include thyroid surgery, tumours and viral illness.

imaging: CT from skull base to mediastinum

referralThresholdReason: Needs cause identified and aspiration risk managed; urgent if airway symptoms.
urgencyRationale: Aspiration and underlying malignancy risk.
patientAdvice: If your voice became weak and you cough when drinking, see a doctor this week. Seek emergency help for difficulty breathing.

accessConsiderations: voice therapy and injection laryngoplasty scarce

name: Laryngeal Cancer
description: Laryngeal cancer arises in the voice box and commonly presents with persistent hoarseness. It is strongly linked to smoking and alcohol. Early cancers are highly curable; late ones cause breathing and swallowing difficulty.
diagnosticClues: irregular mass or leukoplakia on laryngoscopy
referralThresholdReason: Early-stage cure rates are high; delay causes advanced, airway-threatening disease.
urgencyRationale: Malignancy with potential airway compromise.
patientAdvice: Hoarseness lasting more than three weeks, especially if you smoke or drink, needs an urgent throat examination. Do not delay.

name: Globus Pharyngeus
description: Globus is the sensation of a lump or tightness in the throat without a physical obstruction. It is common, harmless and often linked to reflux, stress or muscle tension. Swallowing food usually relieves it.
referralThresholdReason: Benign when no red flags; examine to exclude pathology.
urgencyRationale: Harmless but needs red flag check.
patientAdvice: This sensation is usually harmless. Avoid constant throat clearing and manage stress. See a doctor if you have trouble swallowing, weight loss or a neck lump.
preventionTips: avoid smoking and spicy meals late

localFactors: reflux due to spicy and late meals

name: Dysphagia
description: Dysphagia is difficulty or discomfort swallowing food, liquid or saliva. It may arise from the mouth, throat or oesophagus and has causes ranging from reflux to cancer. It can lead to choking, aspiration and weight loss.
referralThresholdReason: Progressive or persistent dysphagia may indicate malignancy or aspiration.
urgencyRationale: Risk of malnutrition, aspiration and underlying cancer.
patientAdvice: If swallowing is getting harder, you are losing weight or coughing when eating, see a doctor this week. Eat slowly and sit upright for meals.

localFactors: oesophageal cancer and caustic ingestion strictures
accessConsiderations: endoscopy and barium available in few centres

name: Laryngopharyngeal Reflux
description: Laryngopharyngeal reflux occurs when stomach contents reach the throat and voice box, often without heartburn. It causes chronic throat clearing, hoarseness, cough and a lump sensation. It is common and treatable with lifestyle changes and medication.

primary: backflow of gastric acid and pepsin into pharynx

referralThresholdReason: First-line treatment in primary care; refer if refractory or red flags.
urgencyRationale: Benign but chronic; red flags need exclusion of cancer.
patientAdvice: Avoid eating within three hours of bedtime, cut back on spicy or fatty food and raise the head of your bed. See a doctor if there is difficulty swallowing or weight loss.

name: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea
description: Obstructive sleep apnoea is repeated blockage of the upper airway during sleep causing pauses in breathing and fragmented sleep. It causes loud snoring, daytime sleepiness and raised risk of heart disease. Treatment includes lifestyle changes, CPAP and sometimes surgery.

selfCare: avoid alcohol and sedatives at night

referralThresholdReason: Risk of cardiovascular disease and road accidents; severe cases require prompt sleep assessment.
urgencyRationale: Chronic health risk, with driving and cardiovascular danger.
patientAdvice: Lose weight if overweight, avoid alcohol before bed and do not drive when sleepy. See a doctor if you or a partner notices pauses in your breathing during sleep.
preventionTips: avoid alcohol and sedatives at night

name: Snoring
description: Snoring is noisy breathing during sleep caused by vibration of relaxed throat tissues. It can be harmless but may be a sign of sleep apnoea. It is common in overweight people, mouth breathers and those with nasal blockage.

primary: vibration of soft palate and pharyngeal tissues

redFlags: child with poor growth or behaviour problems
referralThresholdReason: Benign unless apnoea suspected.
urgencyRationale: Mostly a nuisance; can mask sleep apnoea.
patientAdvice: Try side sleeping, avoid alcohol near bedtime and lose weight if needed. See a doctor if you stop breathing in sleep or feel very sleepy in the day.

name: Tonsilloliths
description: Tonsil stones are small white or yellow calcified clumps of debris and bacteria trapped in the crypts of the tonsils. They cause bad breath, a feeling of something stuck and sometimes mild throat discomfort. They are harmless but can be recurrent.

primary: white or yellow lumps on tonsils
feeling of something stuck in throat
accumulation of food debris, bacteria and dead cells in tonsil crypts

referralThresholdReason: Benign; surgery only for persistent troublesome cases.
urgencyRationale: Harmless nuisance condition.
patientAdvice: Gargle with salt water and keep your mouth clean. Do not dig them out with sharp objects. See a doctor if one tonsil is swollen or you have pain or bleeding.

name: Retropharyngeal Abscess
description: A retropharyngeal abscess is a pus collection in the space behind the throat, mostly in young children after throat infection. It causes fever, neck stiffness, drooling and painful swallowing. It can obstruct the airway or spread to the chest.
diagnosticClues: widened prevertebral soft tissue on lateral neck X-ray

surgical: external drainage if extends to neck or mediastinum

referralThresholdReason: Airway compromise and mediastinitis can develop rapidly.
urgencyRationale: Life-threatening airway and deep infection risk.
patientAdvice: Go to the emergency department immediately if a child has fever, neck stiffness, drooling or difficulty swallowing or breathing.

name: Ludwig's Angina
description: Ludwig's angina is a rapidly spreading infection of the floor of the mouth and neck, usually from a lower tooth infection. It causes swelling under the jaw, tongue elevation and trouble swallowing and breathing. It is a life-threatening airway emergency.

primary: swelling under the jaw and neck

referralThresholdReason: Airway can close rapidly; mortality high without treatment.
urgencyRationale: Rapid airway obstruction with sepsis risk.
patientAdvice: Go to the emergency department immediately if you have swelling under the jaw, a swollen tongue or trouble swallowing or breathing after a tooth problem.

name: Airway Foreign Body
description: An airway foreign body is an object such as a peanut, seed or toy inhaled into the larynx, trachea or bronchi. It causes sudden choking, coughing and wheeze, and can block breathing entirely. It is common in toddlers and is an emergency.

primary: aspiration of food, seeds or small objects

selfCare: back blows and chest or abdominal thrusts per first-aid training
surgical: tracheostomy or thoracotomy in rare cases

referralThresholdReason: Total obstruction causes death in minutes.
urgencyRationale: Immediate life-threatening airway obstruction.
patientAdvice: If someone is choking and cannot breathe, call emergency services and start first aid right away. Do not put fingers blindly in the mouth. Any child with a choking episode followed by cough needs hospital assessment.
preventionTips: avoid whole nuts and small hard foods under 5 years

localFactors: groundnuts, melon seeds and beans given to toddlers
accessConsiderations: rigid bronchoscopy available in few centres

name: Diphtheria
description: Diphtheria is a bacterial throat infection that forms a thick grey membrane and releases a toxin affecting the heart and nerves. It causes sore throat, fever and a swollen 'bull neck'. It is vaccine-preventable but outbreaks occur where immunisation is low.

primary: grey membrane on tonsils or throat

diagnosticClues: adherent grey-white membrane that bleeds on scraping

laboratory: throat swab culture and toxin testing

referralThresholdReason: Toxin causes heart failure, nerve paralysis and airway obstruction.
urgencyRationale: Life-threatening toxin-mediated disease and public health emergency.
patientAdvice: Seek emergency care immediately if a child has sore throat with a grey coating in the throat, a swollen neck or trouble breathing. Ensure household contacts are assessed.

localFactors: low routine immunisation coverage in some regions

name: Oropharyngeal Candidiasis
description: Oropharyngeal candidiasis is a fungal infection of the mouth and throat causing creamy white patches and soreness. It is common in infants, people using steroid inhalers, and those with diabetes or HIV. It can cause painful swallowing when it extends to the throat.

primary: white patches in mouth or throat

diagnosticClues: removable white plaques on red base

medication: oral fluconazole for severe or pharyngeal disease

referralThresholdReason: Treatable at GP level; investigate underlying cause if recurrent.
urgencyRationale: Usually mild; can signal HIV or diabetes.
patientAdvice: Practice good mouth hygiene and rinse after using steroid inhalers. See a doctor for antifungal treatment and tests if thrush keeps returning.

name: Acute Sialadenitis
description: Sialadenitis is infection or inflammation of a salivary gland, usually the parotid or submandibular gland. It causes painful swelling, often worse at mealtimes, and may produce pus in the mouth. It is commonly linked to dehydration or stones.

primary: painful swollen gland in cheek or under jaw

selfCare: sour sweets or lemon to stimulate saliva

referralThresholdReason: Responds to antibiotics but abscess or underlying stones need review.
urgencyRationale: Painful, can form abscess; rarely airway threatening.
patientAdvice: Drink plenty of fluids, massage the gland and suck sour sweets to stimulate saliva. See a doctor this week for antibiotics. Go to emergency care if swelling spreads or breathing is difficult.

accessConsiderations: often confused with mumps or tooth infection

name: Mumps Parotitis
description: Mumps is a contagious viral infection causing painful swelling of the parotid glands in front of the ears. It produces fever, headache and puffy cheeks. It can cause complications such as deafness, orchitis and meningitis.

primary: swelling in front of and below the ear

diagnosticClues: bilateral parotid swelling with earlobe lift
referralThresholdReason: Self-limiting; refer for complications.
urgencyRationale: Usually self-limiting; complications can be serious.
patientAdvice: Rest, drink fluids and stay away from school or work for five days. Seek medical care for severe headache, neck stiffness, testicular pain or hearing changes.

localFactors: MMR not in routine schedule in many areas

name: Salivary Gland Stones
description: Salivary stones are calcified deposits that block the duct of a salivary gland, most often under the jaw. They cause painful swelling that comes and goes with meals. Stones can lead to infection.

primary: painful swelling under jaw or in cheek at mealtimes
swelling that goes down after eating
calcium salt deposition in salivary duct

clinical: bimanual palpation of floor of mouth

referralThresholdReason: Stones can be treated electively unless infection develops.
urgencyRationale: Uncomfortable, risk of infection.
patientAdvice: Drink plenty of water, suck sour sweets and massage the gland to help pass the stone. See a doctor if you develop fever or spreading swelling.
preventionTips: avoid drugs that dry the mouth if possible

accessConsiderations: stones often missed or mistaken for dental problems

name: Sjogren's Syndrome
commonName: Dry mouth and dry eye disease
description: Sjogren's syndrome is an autoimmune disease that attacks tear and salivary glands, causing dry eyes and dry mouth. It may also cause salivary gland swelling, fatigue and joint pain. It is more common in women and has a small lymphoma risk.

primary: autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands

referralThresholdReason: Chronic disease requiring multidisciplinary care; urgent if lymphoma suspected.
urgencyRationale: Chronic condition with low risk of lymphoma.
patientAdvice: Sip water often, use artificial tears and look after your teeth. See a doctor for blood tests if dry mouth and dry eyes persist.

localFactors: symptoms attributed to ageing or medications

name: Thyroid Mass / Goitre
commonName: Lump in the front of the neck
description: A thyroid mass is a lump or swelling in the thyroid gland at the front of the neck, including goitre and nodules. Most are benign, but some are cancerous. Evaluation includes ultrasound, thyroid function tests and often biopsy.

medication: thyroid hormone replacement or antithyroid drugs

referralThresholdReason: Needs assessment to exclude cancer; urgent if rapid growth, hoarseness or airway symptoms.
urgencyRationale: Usually benign but malignancy must be excluded.
patientAdvice: A neck lump that moves when you swallow should be checked this week. Seek urgent care if it grows quickly, your voice changes or you have trouble breathing.

accessConsiderations: FNAC and thyroid surgery in tertiary centres

name: Cervical Lymphadenopathy
description: Cervical lymphadenopathy is enlargement of lymph nodes in the neck, most often reacting to infections of the throat, mouth or scalp. Persistent, hard or growing nodes may signal TB, lymphoma or cancer. Evaluation depends on size, duration and associated symptoms.

primary: viral and bacterial throat or dental infection

redFlags: node over 2 cm lasting over 3 weeks
diagnosticClues: painless firm matted nodes suggest TB
referralThresholdReason: Persistent nodes over 3 weeks need biopsy to exclude TB, lymphoma and cancer.
urgencyRationale: Usually reactive, but may indicate serious disease.
patientAdvice: Swollen glands with a cold usually settle in two weeks. If a lump lasts over three weeks, is hard, growing or comes with weight loss or night sweats, see a doctor this week.

name: Branchial Cleft Cyst
description: A branchial cleft cyst is a smooth, painless lump on the side of the neck, present from birth but often noticed in childhood or early adulthood. It may enlarge or become infected after an upper respiratory infection. Surgical removal is curative.

primary: painless lump on side of neck
failure of branchial cleft to obliterate in embryo

diagnosticClues: fluctuant lateral neck mass anterior to sternocleidomastoid
referralThresholdReason: Benign; elective excision. In adults, malignancy must be excluded.
urgencyRationale: Benign but can become infected or mimic malignancy in adults.
patientAdvice: A painless neck lump should always be checked. These cysts are harmless but infection can occur. See an ENT doctor to plan removal.

name: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
description: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline neck lump that develops from remnants of the thyroid's embryonic path. It moves upward when swallowing or sticking out the tongue. It may become infected and requires surgical removal.

imaging: thyroid scan if ectopic thyroid suspected

referralThresholdReason: Elective surgery; urgent if infected.
urgencyRationale: Benign but recurrent infection if untreated.
patientAdvice: If you have a midline neck lump that moves when you swallow or stick out your tongue, see an ENT surgeon to plan removal.

accessConsiderations: Sistrunk surgery available in teaching hospitals

name: Deep Neck Space Abscess
description: A deep neck abscess is a pus collection in the spaces of the neck, usually from tonsil, tooth or throat infection. It causes fever, painful swelling, limited neck movement and difficulty swallowing. It may compress the airway or spread to the chest.
referralThresholdReason: Airway obstruction, mediastinitis and sepsis can develop rapidly.
urgencyRationale: Life-threatening infection with airway risk.
patientAdvice: Go to emergency care immediately for painful neck swelling with fever, trouble swallowing or breathing, or reduced jaw opening.
preventionTips: treat dental and throat infections early

name: Cervical Lymphoma
commonName: Lymph node cancer in the neck
description: Lymphoma is a cancer of lymph tissue that frequently presents as a painless, rubbery neck lump. It may be accompanied by night sweats, fever and weight loss. Diagnosis requires biopsy, and treatment is often highly effective.
redFlags: B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss)
referralThresholdReason: Aggressive lymphomas, including Burkitt, grow fast and require prompt treatment.
urgencyRationale: Malignancy; some forms are rapidly progressive.
patientAdvice: A painless, growing neck lump, especially with night sweats or weight loss, needs urgent specialist assessment and biopsy this week.

name: Temporomandibular Joint Disorder
description: Temporomandibular joint disorder involves pain and dysfunction in the jaw joint and chewing muscles. It causes jaw pain, clicking, locking and sometimes ear pain or headaches that mimic ear disease. Most cases settle with conservative care.

secondary: ear pain with normal ear exam

redFlags: inability to open mouth after trauma
referralThresholdReason: Self-limiting in most; ENT and dental review if refractory or ear symptoms unexplained.
urgencyRationale: Benign, pain and function impact only.
patientAdvice: Eat soft foods, avoid chewing gum and try warm compresses on the jaw. See your doctor or dentist if pain or locking persists.

localFactors: chewing hard foods such as bones

name: Tuberculous Cervical Lymphadenitis
description: Tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis (scrofula) is tuberculosis infection of the lymph nodes in the neck. It causes slowly enlarging painless lumps that may form abscesses and sinuses. It is the commonest form of extrapulmonary TB in many parts of Africa.
diagnosticClues: matted firm nodes with cold abscess
caseous necrosis on FNA or biopsy
referralThresholdReason: Needs prompt diagnosis and TB treatment; also to exclude lymphoma.
urgencyRationale: Treatable infection; delays allow spread and complications.
patientAdvice: If neck lumps last for weeks, especially with night sweats or weight loss, get tested for TB and HIV. TB treatment is free in government facilities.

accessConsiderations: free TB treatment available via national programme
FNA and GeneXpert not universally available

name: Parotid Gland Tumour
commonName: Lump in the cheek near the ear
description: Parotid tumours are growths in the salivary gland in front of the ear. Most are benign, such as pleomorphic adenoma, but some are malignant. A painless, slowly growing lump is typical, while facial weakness suggests malignancy.

primary: painless lump in front of or below ear

diagnosticClues: firm mobile mass in parotid tail

surgical: superficial or total parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation

referralThresholdReason: Needs diagnosis to exclude malignancy; benign tumours still need surgery.
urgencyRationale: Mostly benign but malignancy must be excluded.
patientAdvice: A lump near your ear or cheek that is growing or causing facial weakness should be checked this week. Do not massage or squeeze it.
preventionTips: avoid unnecessary head and neck radiation
complications: facial nerve injury from surgery or tumour

name: Bell's Palsy
description: Bell's palsy is a sudden weakness of one side of the face caused by inflammation of the facial nerve. The cause is often viral. Most people improve within weeks to months, especially with early steroid treatment.

primary: sudden weakness of one side of face

diagnosticClues: lower motor neuron pattern including forehead

laboratory: Lyme and HIV serology if indicated
imaging: MRI if atypical or no recovery

selfCare: eye protection with lubricant and patch at night

referralThresholdReason: Steroids work best within 72 hours; stroke and other causes must be excluded.
urgencyRationale: Time-sensitive treatment and exclusion of stroke.
patientAdvice: See a doctor within a day if one side of your face suddenly droops. Protect your eye with drops and tape it shut at night. Call emergency services if you also have arm weakness or slurred speech.

localFactors: often attributed to spiritual causes or cold exposure

name: Oral Cavity Cancer
description: Oral cavity cancer arises in the tongue, gums, floor of mouth or cheek lining. It often presents as a non-healing ulcer, white or red patch or lump. Tobacco, alcohol and betel use are major risks, and early detection greatly improves survival.
referralThresholdReason: Early-stage disease is curable; delay leads to advanced disease.
urgencyRationale: Malignancy needing prompt diagnosis.
patientAdvice: A mouth ulcer or lump that has not healed in three weeks needs a biopsy. See a specialist this week. Stop smoking and chewing tobacco.

name: Laryngomalacia
description: Laryngomalacia is a common congenital condition in which soft laryngeal tissue collapses inward during breathing, causing noisy breathing (stridor) in infants. It usually appears in the first weeks of life and improves by 12-18 months. Severe cases cause feeding and growth problems.

primary: worse when feeding, crying or lying on back
immature laryngeal cartilage and supraglottic collapse

redFlags: stridor present at rest or biphasic
referralThresholdReason: Mild cases resolve; urgent if feeding, growth or breathing is compromised.
urgencyRationale: Mostly benign; severe forms threaten growth and breathing.
patientAdvice: Feed your baby upright and in small amounts. See a doctor for noisy breathing. Go to emergency care if the baby turns blue, struggles to breathe or stops feeding.

localFactors: often thought to be spiritual or asthma

name: Glue Ear in Children
description: Glue ear in children is persistent sticky fluid behind the eardrum causing mild to moderate hearing loss. It commonly occurs between ages 2 and 7 and often follows colds or ear infections. It may affect speech, behaviour and schooling if prolonged.
diagnosticClues: mild conductive hearing loss on audiometry

selfCare: seat child near front of class

referralThresholdReason: Review at 3 months; earlier if speech or learning concerns.
urgencyRationale: Non-dangerous but affects development.
patientAdvice: Many children get better by themselves. Speak clearly, face your child and tell the teacher about their hearing. See an ENT doctor if it lasts beyond three months.

name: Adenotonsillar Hypertrophy
description: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is enlargement of both tonsils and adenoids in children. It causes snoring, mouth breathing, restless sleep and sometimes sleep apnoea. Removal is considered when breathing during sleep is affected.
referralThresholdReason: Sleep apnoea affects growth, behaviour and heart; referral if apnoea suspected.
urgencyRationale: Can cause significant sleep-disordered breathing.
patientAdvice: If your child snores loudly or pauses breathing at night, see an ENT doctor. Record a short video of the sleep breathing to show the doctor.

accessConsiderations: adenotonsillectomy in teaching and private hospitals

name: Paediatric Hearing Loss
description: Paediatric hearing loss is reduced hearing in a child from many causes, including fluid, infection, genetics or nerve damage. Even mild loss can delay speech, language and learning. Early detection and intervention are critical.

imaging: MRI or CT temporal bones if sensorineural

referralThresholdReason: Early intervention before age 6 months achieves best speech outcomes.
urgencyRationale: Language development window is time-limited.
patientAdvice: If your child does not react to sounds, is not babbling or is slow to speak, arrange a hearing test as soon as possible. Early help makes a big difference.

accessConsiderations: hearing aids and speech therapy costly

name: Recurrent Acute Otitis Media
description: Recurrent acute otitis media is three or more ear infections in six months or four in a year. It is most common in young children and may indicate Eustachian tube problems, adenoid disease or allergy. Grommets may be offered when episodes are frequent.
referralThresholdReason: Surgical prevention considered after 3 episodes in 6 months or 4 in 12 months.
urgencyRationale: Repeated infection risks hearing and development.
patientAdvice: Record each ear infection and see an ENT specialist if your child has had three in six months. Complete all prescribed antibiotics.

name: Congenital Hearing Loss
description: Congenital hearing loss is hearing loss present at birth, caused by genetic factors, infections during pregnancy or birth complications. It may affect one or both ears. Early detection and intervention allow near-normal language development.

primary: no startle response to loud sounds

referralThresholdReason: Intervention before 6 months of age gives best language outcomes.
urgencyRationale: Critical developmental window for language.
patientAdvice: If your newborn failed a hearing test or does not respond to sounds, see a paediatric ENT or audiologist without delay. Early support protects your child's language.

name: Persistent Middle Ear Effusion Requiring Grommets
description: This entry covers children whose persistent fluid in the middle ear or recurrent infections meet criteria for grommet (ventilation tube) insertion. Grommets drain fluid, equalise pressure and improve hearing. They usually fall out on their own after 6-12 months.

primary: fluid behind eardrum for over 3 months

diagnosticClues: bilateral type B tympanogram for 3 months

selfCare: keep ears dry as advised after surgery

referralThresholdReason: Elective surgery after 3 months of documented effusion with hearing loss or frequent infections.
urgencyRationale: Elective but important for speech and learning.
patientAdvice: If your child has had fluid in the ear and poor hearing for three months, ask for an ENT assessment. Tubes are a short quick procedure that often improves hearing.
keywords: fluid in child ear for months

name: Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis
description: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is a condition where HPV causes wart-like growths on the vocal cords and airway. In children it causes progressive hoarseness and noisy breathing, and growths often return after removal. It requires repeated surgery and specialist care.

primary: progressive hoarse voice or weak cry

diagnosticClues: warty exophytic growths on vocal cords on laryngoscopy

imaging: chest X-ray or CT if distal spread

selfCare: HPV vaccination of household where applicable
medication: adjuvant antiviral or bevacizumab in aggressive disease

referralThresholdReason: Airway can narrow progressively; urgent if stridor or distress.
urgencyRationale: Chronic airway threat requiring repeated procedures.
patientAdvice: A child with persistent hoarseness or noisy breathing should have their voice box examined. Go to emergency care if breathing becomes difficult.

localFactors: late diagnosis often mistaken for asthma

name: Oesophageal Foreign Body
commonName: Swallowed object stuck in food pipe
description: An oesophageal foreign body is an object or food bolus lodged in the swallowing tube. It causes pain, drooling and inability to swallow. Sharp objects, button batteries and magnets are emergencies due to the risk of perforation.

primary: something stuck in throat or chest
swallowed coins, bones, food bolus, batteries

redFlags: chest or neck pain with fever

laboratory: full blood count if perforation suspected

selfCare: do not induce vomiting or eat
surgical: surgical removal for perforation or impaction

referralThresholdReason: Risk of perforation, mediastinitis and fatal vascular injury, especially with batteries.
urgencyRationale: Time-critical for batteries, sharp objects and complete obstruction.
patientAdvice: Go to the emergency department immediately if you or your child may have swallowed a battery, sharp object or cannot swallow saliva. Do not eat or drink and do not induce vomiting.
preventionTips: keep coins and batteries away from children

accessConsiderations: traditional remedies such as swallowing bread or plantain

name: Eustachian Tube Dysfunction
description: The tube linking the middle ear to the back of the nose fails to open properly, so pressure cannot equalise. This causes a blocked or full feeling, muffled hearing and popping or crackling sounds. It is often linked to colds, allergies and sinus problems.
typicalDuration: days to weeks; can be chronic
redFlags: one-sided blocked ear with a neck lump in an adult

imaging: CT or MRI nasopharynx if persistent one-sided in adult

selfCare: swallow or yawn to open tubes
medication: oral or nasal decongestant (short course only)

referralThresholdReason: Usually self-limiting. Needs ENT review if it lasts more than 6 weeks, is one-sided in an adult, or hearing drops.
urgencyRationale: Uncomfortable but rarely harmful; persistent one-sided cases in adults need a nasopharyngeal tumour excluded.
patientAdvice: Try swallowing, yawning and chewing gum. Treat any nose allergy or cold. See a doctor if the blocked feeling lasts more than a month or only one ear is affected.
preventionTips: do not fly with a heavy cold

localFactors: heavy exposure to smoke from cooking fires
accessConsiderations: audiometry and tympanometry limited outside tertiary centres

name: Furuncle of the External Ear Canal
description: A painful localised staphylococcal infection of a hair follicle in the outer part of the ear canal. It causes severe pain that worsens when the ear is touched or pulled. It may burst with a little pus.

primary: pain on touching or pulling the ear

redFlags: poorly controlled diabetes with severe ear pain
diagnosticClues: narrowed canal with normal deep canal

medication: topical antibiotic or antiseptic ear drops
oral antibiotic active against staphylococci if spreading

referralThresholdReason: Usually settles with GP treatment. Seen sooner if diabetic, rapidly spreading or very painful.
urgencyRationale: Very painful but rarely dangerous; diabetics need prompt care to exclude malignant otitis externa.
patientAdvice: Apply a warm compress and take pain relief. Do not poke the ear. See a doctor this week, or sooner if you have diabetes or the swelling spreads.
preventionTips: do not clean ears with sharp objects

localFactors: use of sticks, hairpins and matchsticks to clean ears

name: Auricular Keloid
description: An overgrowth of firm scar tissue that extends beyond the original wound on the earlobe or ear after piercing or injury. It is not cancerous but can grow large, itch, hurt and cause distress. It frequently returns after simple removal.

primary: firm raised lump on earlobe or ear
abnormal wound healing after piercing or trauma

diagnosticClues: firm rubbery smooth nodule at piercing site

surgical: surgical excision combined with adjuvant therapy
