referralThresholdReason: Not dangerous but recurrence is common; best managed by ENT or plastic surgeon with adjuvant treatment.
urgencyRationale: Benign and non-urgent; plan treatment to limit recurrence.
patientAdvice: Do not cut the lump yourself or have it removed at an unlicensed clinic, as it will usually grow back bigger. See an ENT or plastic surgeon about steroid injections or combined treatment.
preventionTips: avoid ear piercing if prone to keloids

localFactors: keloids common in people with dark skin
accessConsiderations: traditional or local excision commonly leads to recurrence
steroid injections and radiotherapy available in few centres

name: Ototoxic Hearing Loss and Balance Damage
description: Damage to the hearing or balance organs of the inner ear caused by certain medicines or chemicals. It usually causes high-pitched hearing loss with tinnitus, and sometimes unsteadiness. Damage is often permanent.

primary: progressive hearing loss in both ears

typicalDuration: days to weeks after exposure; often permanent

primary: quinine and chloroquine at high dose

redFlags: sudden hearing loss during drug treatment
diagnosticClues: bilateral symmetrical high-frequency loss on audiometry

selfCare: report ringing or dizziness to the prescriber
medication: review or substitute the offending drug

referralThresholdReason: Early recognition during drug treatment can prevent progression; stop or change drug under medical supervision.
urgencyRationale: Permanent loss can occur quickly; prompt drug review limits damage.
patientAdvice: If you develop ringing in the ears, hearing loss or dizziness while taking antibiotic injections, chemotherapy or quinine, tell your doctor immediately and do not stop treatment on your own without advice.
complications: speech and learning problems in children

localFactors: widespread use of gentamicin injections and quinine for malaria
accessConsiderations: no routine hearing monitoring on chemotherapy

name: Hyperacusis
description: Everyday sounds that are normally comfortable seem painfully loud or intolerable. It may follow noise exposure, head injury, or occur with tinnitus and anxiety. Hearing is usually normal on testing.

primary: discomfort or pain with everyday noise
cochlear or central auditory gain abnormality

diagnosticClues: lowered loudness discomfort levels with normal hearing thresholds

imaging: MRI if asymmetric or neurological signs

selfCare: avoid wearing earplugs all the time
medication: treat underlying anxiety or depression where present

referralThresholdReason: Not dangerous; benefits from specialist sound therapy and counselling.
urgencyRationale: Quality-of-life condition without risk to life.
patientAdvice: Avoid constantly blocking out sound with earplugs, which makes it worse. See an audiologist for guided sound therapy.

localFactors: generator noise and loud religious and social events
accessConsiderations: often misread as anxiety or spiritual problem

name: Pulsatile Tinnitus
description: Hearing a rhythmic whooshing or thumping in time with the heartbeat. It may be caused by blood vessel problems, raised pressure in the head, or anaemia, and sometimes by a tumour near the ear. It needs assessment because some causes are serious.

primary: rhythmic whooshing or thumping in ear

diagnosticClues: red or blue mass behind eardrum

medication: acetazolamide in specialist care for raised intracranial pressure
surgical: surgery or stenting for vascular lesions or tumours

referralThresholdReason: Some causes are vascular or neoplastic and need imaging; not usually immediately life-threatening.
urgencyRationale: Treatable causes must be found early; sudden onset with neurology is an emergency.
patientAdvice: See a doctor this week to check your blood pressure and blood count. Go to hospital urgently if there is sudden vision loss, severe headache or facial weakness.

localFactors: anaemia from malaria and poor nutrition
accessConsiderations: imaging such as MR angiography limited to few centres

name: Temporal Bone Fracture
description: A fracture of the skull bone housing the ear, usually after a head injury, road traffic accident or fall. It can damage the hearing organ, balance organ and facial nerve, and may cause leakage of brain fluid. It is a medical emergency because of associated head injury.

primary: bleeding from ear after head injury
secondary: clear fluid from ear or nose

imaging: CT head and high-resolution CT temporal bones

selfCare: do not clean or plug the ear
medication: steroids for facial palsy in selected cases

referralThresholdReason: Associated brain injury and meningitis risk; needs immediate hospital evaluation.
urgencyRationale: Life-threatening head injury and facial nerve or meningitis risk.
patientAdvice: Go to the emergency department immediately after any head injury with blood or clear fluid from the ear. Do not put anything in the ear.

localFactors: high rates of motorcycle taxi crashes without helmets
accessConsiderations: CT scanners concentrated in urban centres

name: Superior Semicircular Canal Dehiscence
description: A thin or missing area of bone over a balance canal in the inner ear creates an abnormal 'third window'. People may hear their own heartbeat or eye movements, and loud sounds or pressure changes can trigger dizziness. It is uncommon and often mistaken for other balance disorders.

primary: dizziness triggered by loud sounds or pressure
autophony (hearing own voice or heartbeat loudly)
hearing own footsteps or eye movements
thinning or absence of bone over superior semicircular canal

redFlags: none specific; seek care if sudden severe vertigo or hearing loss
diagnosticClues: conductive hearing loss with intact reflexes

surgical: canal plugging or resurfacing by neurotologist

referralThresholdReason: Disabling but not dangerous; confirm with CT and VEMP.
urgencyRationale: Chronic and disabling but non-urgent.
patientAdvice: See an ENT balance specialist if loud noise or pressure makes you dizzy. Avoid known triggers and protect against falls.

accessConsiderations: specialist neurotology and VEMP testing almost unavailable

name: Autoimmune Inner Ear Disease
description: The immune system attacks the inner ear, causing rapidly progressive hearing loss in both ears over weeks to months. Balance problems and ear fullness may occur. It often responds to steroids if caught early.

primary: progressive hearing loss in both ears

diagnosticClues: bilateral asymmetric SNHL progressing over weeks
referralThresholdReason: Early steroid therapy preserves hearing; delay risks permanent loss.
urgencyRationale: Rapid progression needs timely diagnosis.
patientAdvice: Rapidly worsening hearing in both ears needs urgent testing. See an ENT doctor within a few days.

localFactors: under-diagnosed because autoimmune screens are limited
accessConsiderations: steroids often given by non-specialists without audiometry

name: Otogenic Intracranial Complications
commonName: Ear infection spreading to the brain
description: Serious spread of ear infection into the skull, causing meningitis, brain abscess or venous sinus thrombosis. It usually follows chronic or acute ear or mastoid infection. It is life-threatening and needs emergency treatment.

primary: spread of infection via bone or blood vessels

redFlags: sudden worsening after ear discharge stopped
referralThresholdReason: High mortality without immediate treatment.
urgencyRationale: Immediately life-threatening.
patientAdvice: Go to the emergency department at once if an ear infection is accompanied by severe headache, stiff neck, drowsiness or confusion.
preventionTips: seek ENT care for ear discharge lasting more than 2 weeks

localFactors: chronic ear infections untreated for years

name: Vestibular Migraine
description: Recurring episodes of vertigo or unsteadiness linked to migraine, with or without headache. Attacks last minutes to days and may include sensitivity to light and sound. It is a common but under-recognised cause of dizziness.
riskFactors: personal or family history of migraine

imaging: MRI if atypical or neurological signs

referralThresholdReason: Not dangerous but needs correct diagnosis to avoid unnecessary treatment.
urgencyRationale: Recurrent and disabling but not life-threatening.
patientAdvice: Keep a diary of dizzy spells and triggers. See a doctor if attacks are frequent. Go to hospital if dizziness comes with weakness, speech trouble or double vision.

localFactors: common but misdiagnosed as malaria, 'high blood' or 'weak blood'

name: Post-Meningitic Hearing Loss
description: Permanent sensorineural hearing loss following bacterial meningitis, caused by infection of the inner ear. It may affect one or both ears and can progress to profound deafness. Early hearing tests after meningitis are important.

primary: poor response to sound in a child

imaging: MRI temporal bone for cochlear ossification

referralThresholdReason: Early implantation within weeks to months preserves outcomes, so hearing testing should follow any meningitis.
urgencyRationale: Time-sensitive for cochlear implant candidacy.
patientAdvice: If your child has had meningitis, get a hearing test as soon as they have recovered.
preventionTips: vaccination against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae and meningococcus

accessConsiderations: hearing testing after meningitis rarely done
cochlear implant extremely limited and costly

name: Lassa Fever Sensorineural Hearing Loss
description: Sudden or progressive sensorineural hearing loss occurring during or after Lassa fever, a viral haemorrhagic illness spread by rodents. It affects a large proportion of survivors and is often permanent. Hearing loss may appear as the illness improves.

primary: hearing loss in one or both ears
Lassa virus damage to inner ear

redFlags: acute fever with bleeding or confusion
diagnosticClues: bilateral or unilateral SNHL during convalescence
referralThresholdReason: Early steroid and audiometric assessment may preserve hearing.
urgencyRationale: Sudden hearing loss is time-sensitive.
patientAdvice: If you lost hearing after Lassa fever or a severe fever, see an ENT doctor for a hearing test quickly.

localFactors: endemic in Edo, Ondo, Ebonyi, Bauchi
accessConsiderations: survivors often not offered hearing tests

name: Preauricular Sinus
description: A small pit or tract in front of the ear present from birth, caused by incomplete fusion of ear structures. It is often harmless but can become infected, forming a swelling or discharging abscess.

primary: small pit in front of ear

diagnosticClues: small epithelial-lined pit near the helix
referralThresholdReason: Surgery considered only for recurrent infection.
urgencyRationale: Benign unless infected.
patientAdvice: A pit with no symptoms needs no treatment. See a doctor if it becomes red, painful or discharges.

localFactors: commonly noticed in infants and often left untreated
accessConsiderations: surgical expertise limited in rural areas

name: Microtia and Aural Atresia
description: A congenital malformation where the outer ear is small or misshapen (microtia) and the ear canal may be absent (atresia). Hearing is often reduced on the affected side. Early hearing assessment is important.

primary: developmental malformation of first and second branchial arches

redFlags: none specific; seek care if infection or poor development

imaging: CT temporal bone from around age 5

referralThresholdReason: Not urgent but early hearing support matters for speech development.
urgencyRationale: Non-emergency but time-sensitive for hearing.
patientAdvice: Have your child's hearing tested early. Hearing aids on a soft band can help speech and learning development.

localFactors: stigma and spiritual beliefs about birth defects

name: Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis
description: An allergic reaction to fungi in the sinuses leading to thick, sticky mucus, polyps and gradual sinus blockage. It occurs mainly in young adults with asthma or allergies and is common in warm climates. It is not an invasive infection.

surgical: functional endoscopic sinus surgery to clear mucin

referralThresholdReason: Not acutely dangerous; needs surgery plus medical therapy and follow-up.
urgencyRationale: Chronic but can erode bone and affect orbit if neglected.
patientAdvice: Use saline rinses and see an ENT doctor if you have long-standing nasal blockage with thick discharge or polyps.

localFactors: harmattan dust and high spore loads

name: Acute Invasive Fungal Sinusitis
commonName: Mucormycosis of the nose and sinuses
description: A rapidly spreading, life-threatening fungal infection of the nose and sinuses that invades blood vessels and bone. It mostly affects people with uncontrolled diabetes or weak immunity. Black dead tissue in the nose or palate is a hallmark.

primary: black discharge or crust in nose

typicalDuration: days; progresses within hours to days
redFlags: black dead tissue in nose or palate

imaging: urgent CT or MRI sinuses and orbit
specialist: tissue biopsy with fungal stain and culture

surgical: extensive surgical debridement including orbital exenteration if needed

referralThresholdReason: High mortality; each hour of delay worsens outcome.
urgencyRationale: Rapidly fatal without prompt surgery and antifungals.
patientAdvice: Go to the emergency department immediately if you have diabetes and develop facial pain, black crust in the nose, swelling or vision changes.

localFactors: high prevalence of undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes

name: Nasal Vestibulitis
description: Infection of the skin just inside the nostril, often from picking, plucking hairs or frequent blowing. It causes redness, soreness and crusting, and can form a boil. Spread of infection from the nose to the brain is rare but dangerous.

primary: redness and swelling at nose entrance

referralThresholdReason: Face veins drain to the brain; do not squeeze boils; seek care if spreading.
urgencyRationale: Usually mild but can lead to cavernous sinus thrombosis.
patientAdvice: Do not squeeze or pick. Apply a warm compress and see a doctor if swelling spreads to the face or eye.

name: Nasal Septal Perforation
description: A hole through the wall dividing the two sides of the nose. It can cause crusting, nosebleeds, whistling when breathing and a blocked feeling. It may follow surgery, trauma, drug use or inflammatory disease.
referralThresholdReason: Usually non-urgent; investigate cause if progressive.
urgencyRationale: Symptomatic but rarely dangerous.
patientAdvice: Keep the nose moist with saline and ointment. See an ENT doctor to check for an underlying cause.
preventionTips: avoid nose picking and drug use

name: Sinonasal Inverted Papilloma
description: A benign but locally aggressive tumour arising from the lining of the nose and sinuses, usually on one side. It causes persistent blocked nose and nosebleeds. It can recur and occasionally becomes malignant.
diagnosticClues: polypoid unilateral mass on lateral nasal wall
referralThresholdReason: Unilateral polyp needs biopsy to exclude malignancy.
urgencyRationale: Locally aggressive with malignant potential.
patientAdvice: A blocked nose or bleeding on one side that does not clear needs specialist examination.

accessConsiderations: biopsy and endoscopic surgery limited to tertiary hospitals

name: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma
description: A benign but highly vascular tumour at the back of the nose in adolescent males. It causes recurrent heavy nosebleeds and nasal blockage. Biopsy in clinic is dangerous because of severe bleeding.
referralThresholdReason: Can bleed massively; needs urgent referral.
urgencyRationale: Severe bleeding risk.
patientAdvice: Teenage boys with repeated heavy nosebleeds and a blocked nose need urgent specialist assessment. Do not allow biopsy in a local clinic.
keywords: blocked nose with bleeding in boy

name: Cerebrospinal Fluid Rhinorrhoea
commonName: Clear fluid leaking from the nose
description: Leakage of brain fluid through a defect in the skull base into the nose, producing a persistent watery drip. It follows trauma, surgery or occasionally occurs spontaneously. It carries a risk of meningitis.
referralThresholdReason: Risk of meningitis requires prompt evaluation.
urgencyRationale: Meningitis risk.
patientAdvice: If clear fluid drips from your nose after head injury, see a doctor immediately. Seek emergency care if you have fever, neck stiffness or severe headache.
keywords: fluid from nose after head injury

localFactors: head injury from road traffic collisions
accessConsiderations: beta-2 transferrin testing unavailable in most centres

name: Hereditary Haemorrhagic Telangiectasia
description: An inherited condition causing fragile blood vessels in the nose and elsewhere, leading to frequent spontaneous nosebleeds. It may cause anaemia and bleeding in other organs. Family history is common.

primary: red spots on lips or fingers

referralThresholdReason: Chronic condition; urgent only with heavy bleeding.
urgencyRationale: Recurrent bleeding and anaemia risk.
patientAdvice: Keep the nose moist and see your doctor regularly for blood checks. Go to hospital for bleeding that does not stop after 15 minutes of pressure.

name: Rhinoscleroma
description: A slowly progressive infection of the nose caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, leading to crusting, nasal obstruction and hard nasal swelling. It may extend to the throat and larynx. It is rare but reported in parts of Africa.

medication: long course of antibiotics (tetracycline or fluoroquinolone)

referralThresholdReason: Needs prolonged antibiotics and can threaten airway.
urgencyRationale: Progressive disease.
patientAdvice: Seek specialist care for long-term nasal blockage with crusting and nasal deformity.

name: Inferior Turbinate Hypertrophy
description: Enlargement of the lower nasal turbinates causes persistent nasal blockage that alternates between sides. It results from allergies, irritants or long-term decongestant use.
referralThresholdReason: Non-urgent; treat medically first.
urgencyRationale: Quality of life only.
patientAdvice: Use saline rinses and prescribed nasal sprays. See ENT if there is no improvement.
keywords: nose blocked on one side then other

name: Infectious Mononucleosis
description: A viral illness caused mainly by Epstein-Barr virus, producing severe sore throat, swollen glands and marked tiredness. It is most common in teenagers and young adults. The spleen may enlarge and fatigue can last weeks.

medication: short-course steroids in severe airway swelling

referralThresholdReason: Mostly self-limiting; seek urgent care if airway compromise.
urgencyRationale: Usually benign but can cause airway swelling.
patientAdvice: Rest, drink plenty of fluids and avoid contact sports. Seek urgent care if breathing or swallowing becomes difficult.

accessConsiderations: often mislabelled as malaria or typhoid

name: Lemierre Syndrome
commonName: Throat infection with blood clot in neck vein
description: A rare but life-threatening complication of throat infection where the internal jugular vein becomes infected and clots, spreading bacteria to the lungs and other organs. It typically follows a sore throat or tonsillitis.

primary: sore throat followed by neck pain

referralThresholdReason: Septic emboli can be rapidly fatal.
urgencyRationale: Life-threatening sepsis.
patientAdvice: Seek emergency care if sore throat is followed by neck swelling with high fever and chills.
preventionTips: complete antibiotic courses for severe sore throats
keywords: sore throat then neck swelling with fever

name: Muscle Tension Dysphonia
description: A voice disorder caused by excessive tension of the muscles around the voice box, leading to hoarseness, vocal fatigue and a tight throat feeling. The vocal cords are usually normal.
redFlags: hoarseness longer than 3 weeks in smokers
diagnosticClues: normal vocal cords with tense posture
referralThresholdReason: Voice therapy is key; examine larynx to exclude pathology.
urgencyRationale: Non-urgent functional.
patientAdvice: Rest your voice, drink water, avoid shouting and whispering. Seek review if hoarseness lasts more than 3 weeks.

localFactors: preaching, teaching and market trading with loud voice use

name: Spasmodic Dysphonia
description: A neurological disorder in which vocal cords go into involuntary spasm during speech, giving a strained, broken or breathy voice. The voice is often normal when laughing or singing.
diagnosticClues: normal cords at rest with spasm on speech
referralThresholdReason: Not dangerous; specialist care improves voice.
urgencyRationale: Chronic non-urgent.
patientAdvice: Voice problems that persist need specialist evaluation. Botulinum toxin injections can help.

accessConsiderations: botulinum toxin costly and unavailable outside major centres

name: Reinke Oedema
description: Fluid swelling of the vocal cords giving a deep, husky voice. It is strongly linked to smoking and voice strain, and most often affects women.
referralThresholdReason: Hoarseness in smokers needs laryngoscopy to exclude cancer.
urgencyRationale: Cancer must be excluded.
patientAdvice: Stop smoking now. Hoarseness lasting more than three weeks needs specialist examination.

name: Laryngeal Trauma
description: Injury to the voice box or windpipe from blunt or penetrating trauma. It can cause voice change, breathing difficulty and bleeding. The airway can deteriorate rapidly.
referralThresholdReason: Airway can collapse suddenly.
urgencyRationale: Immediate airway threat.
patientAdvice: Call for emergency help if there is neck trauma with noisy breathing or voice change.

name: Subglottic Stenosis
commonName: Narrowing of the windpipe below the voice box
description: Narrowing of the airway just beneath the vocal cords, either congenital or after prolonged intubation. It causes noisy breathing and breathlessness.
referralThresholdReason: Airway compromise potential.
urgencyRationale: Potential respiratory failure.
patientAdvice: Noisy breathing after intubation needs urgent medical review.

name: Zenker Diverticulum
description: A pouch forming at the junction between throat and food pipe in older adults. It traps food, causing regurgitation, gurgling and bad breath.
referralThresholdReason: Progressive but not acute.
urgencyRationale: Aspiration risk.
patientAdvice: See an ENT or gastro specialist for swallowing difficulty with regurgitation.

name: Caustic Ingestion Injury
description: Burns to the mouth, throat and food pipe caused by swallowing strong acids, alkalis or household chemicals. It causes immediate pain, drooling and difficulty swallowing and can lead to airway swelling, perforation and later strictures.

selfCare: do not give anything by mouth

referralThresholdReason: Perforation and airway oedema can be fatal.
urgencyRationale: Life-threatening.
patientAdvice: Go to the emergency department at once. Do not induce vomiting or give food or drink.
preventionTips: store chemicals in labelled containers away from children

localFactors: caustic soda used for soap making

name: Hypopharyngeal Cancer
description: A cancer of the lower throat behind the voice box. It causes persistent sore throat, difficulty and pain swallowing, ear pain and neck lumps. It is often diagnosed late.
diagnosticClues: pooling of saliva in pyriform fossa
referralThresholdReason: Early diagnosis improves survival.
urgencyRationale: Rapidly progressive.
patientAdvice: Persistent sore throat, trouble swallowing or ear pain on one side for more than three weeks needs urgent ENT review.

name: Oropharyngeal Cancer
commonName: Cancer of the tonsil or back of the tongue
description: A cancer of the tonsils, base of tongue or soft palate. It may present as a persistent sore throat, one-sided tonsil swelling or neck lump. HPV-related types are increasing.

primary: persistent sore throat on one side

referralThresholdReason: Early treatment improves survival.
urgencyRationale: Suspected cancer.
patientAdvice: One-sided sore throat or neck lump lasting over 3 weeks needs urgent assessment.

name: Upper Airway Angioedema
commonName: Swelling of lips, tongue or throat
description: Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue, face or throat from allergic reactions, drug reactions or inherited disorders. It can block the airway and is a medical emergency.

primary: swelling of lips, tongue or face

referralThresholdReason: Airway obstruction can occur within minutes.
urgencyRationale: Rapid airway threat.
patientAdvice: Seek emergency care immediately if lips, tongue or throat swell or you have trouble breathing.

name: Post-Tonsillectomy Haemorrhage
description: Bleeding from the throat after tonsil removal, either within 24 hours or 5-10 days later when scabs separate. It can be sudden and heavy and needs urgent medical attention.
referralThresholdReason: Large bleeds can be fatal.
urgencyRationale: Risk of shock.
patientAdvice: Go to hospital immediately if there is any bleeding after tonsil surgery.

localFactors: tonsillectomy often done in district hospitals

name: Laryngeal Tuberculosis
description: A tuberculosis infection of the larynx causing hoarseness, painful swallowing and cough. It is often secondary to lung TB and highly infectious.
referralThresholdReason: Needs TB treatment and contact tracing.
urgencyRationale: Infectious with airway risk.
patientAdvice: Persistent hoarseness with cough and weight loss needs TB testing.

accessConsiderations: TB services free but diagnosis delayed

name: Burkitt Lymphoma of the Jaw
description: A very fast-growing cancer of lymphoid tissue, classically presenting as a rapidly enlarging jaw or facial swelling in African children. It is linked to Epstein-Barr virus and malaria and responds well to chemotherapy if treated early.

primary: rapidly growing jaw or facial swelling

referralThresholdReason: Doubles in size in days; early chemotherapy cures most cases.
urgencyRationale: Rapid progression.
patientAdvice: Take a child with a rapidly growing jaw swelling to a hospital immediately; early chemotherapy can cure.

name: Noma (Cancrum Oris)
commonName: Gangrene of the mouth and face
description: A rapidly destructive gangrenous infection of the mouth and face that mainly affects malnourished young children. It starts as a gum ulcer and quickly destroys cheek, lips and bone, with high mortality if untreated.

primary: necrotising infection with fusiform bacteria and spirochaetes

referralThresholdReason: Mortality up to 90 percent untreated.
urgencyRationale: Fatal without treatment.
patientAdvice: Go to hospital immediately if a child has a mouth ulcer with cheek swelling or foul smell.

name: Ranula
description: A fluid-filled cyst on the floor of the mouth from a blocked or leaking salivary gland. It forms a bluish translucent swelling under the tongue and may extend into the neck.

primary: obstruction or rupture of sublingual gland

referralThresholdReason: Benign; surgery for recurrence.
urgencyRationale: Benign.
patientAdvice: See an ENT or oral surgeon if swelling persists.

name: Cystic Hygroma (Lymphatic Malformation)
description: A soft, fluid-filled swelling in the neck or face present from birth or early childhood due to lymphatic malformation. It may enlarge suddenly with infection or bleeding.
referralThresholdReason: Airway risk if enlarging.
urgencyRationale: Potential airway involvement.
patientAdvice: Seek medical review for any newborn neck lump; emergency care if breathing becomes difficult.

name: Infantile Haemangioma
description: A benign blood vessel growth that appears in the first weeks of life, grows rapidly for months, then slowly shrinks. Those near the airway, eye or mouth may need treatment.
referralThresholdReason: Early treatment prevents complications.
urgencyRationale: Mostly benign.
patientAdvice: Take babies with red growths near the eyes, mouth or noisy breathing to a doctor quickly.

name: Thyroid Cancer
description: A malignant growth in the thyroid presenting as a painless neck lump. Most types grow slowly and respond well to treatment, but some are aggressive.

primary: papillary, follicular, medullary or anaplastic carcinoma

referralThresholdReason: Needs prompt evaluation.
urgencyRationale: Possible cancer.
patientAdvice: See a specialist for a new neck lump or hoarse voice.

name: Multinodular Goitre
description: A long-standing enlargement of the thyroid gland with multiple nodules, often due to iodine deficiency. It can cause neck swelling and compress the windpipe or food pipe.
diagnosticClues: firm nodular goitre moving on swallowing
referralThresholdReason: Slowly progressive.
urgencyRationale: Mostly benign.
patientAdvice: See your doctor for gradual neck swelling.

name: Ankyloglossia (Tongue-Tie)
description: A short or tight band under the tongue that restricts tongue movement, sometimes affecting breastfeeding or speech.
referralThresholdReason: Treat only if symptomatic.
urgencyRationale: Benign.
patientAdvice: See a doctor if breastfeeding is painful or the baby is not gaining weight.

name: Cleft Lip and Palate
description: A birth defect where the upper lip or palate fails to fuse during pregnancy. It affects feeding, hearing, speech and appearance, and requires multidisciplinary care.
referralThresholdReason: Early surgery improves feeding and speech.
urgencyRationale: Needs early care.
patientAdvice: Seek early referral for feeding support and surgery planning.

accessConsiderations: charity cleft missions provide free surgery

name: Pierre Robin Sequence
commonName: Small jaw with cleft palate in newborns
description: A newborn condition with a small lower jaw, a tongue positioned too far back and a cleft palate, which can cause breathing and feeding problems.
referralThresholdReason: Risk of airway obstruction.
urgencyRationale: Airway risk.
patientAdvice: Take newborns with noisy breathing or cyanosis to a hospital immediately.

name: Paediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnoea
description: Repeated airway blockage during sleep in children, usually due to enlarged tonsils and adenoids. It causes snoring, restless sleep and daytime behaviour or learning problems.
referralThresholdReason: Can affect growth and heart.
urgencyRationale: Developmental effects.
patientAdvice: Seek review if your child snores nightly with breathing pauses.

name: Paediatric Sinusitis
description: Infection of the sinuses in children typically after a cold, causing prolonged nasal discharge, cough and facial discomfort.

primary: nasal discharge for more than 10 days

referralThresholdReason: Most resolve; urgent if complications.
urgencyRationale: Usually mild.
patientAdvice: Use saline sprays; return if symptoms last beyond 10 days or eye swelling appears.

name: HIV-Related ENT Manifestations
description: HIV commonly causes persistent mouth and throat candidiasis, enlarged neck glands, recurrent ear and sinus infections, parotid swelling and tumours like Kaposi sarcoma.
referralThresholdReason: Early testing and treatment improve outcomes.
urgencyRationale: Needs HIV care.
patientAdvice: Get an HIV test if you have recurrent oral thrush or neck swellings.

name: Odontogenic Facial Space Infection
commonName: Spreading dental abscess in the face
description: Infection from a decayed tooth that spreads into the soft tissues of the face and neck, causing swelling, trismus and sometimes airway compromise.
referralThresholdReason: Rapid airway risk.
urgencyRationale: Potentially life-threatening.
patientAdvice: Seek urgent dental or hospital care for toothache with facial swelling or trouble opening your mouth.

name: Cervicofacial Necrotising Fasciitis
description: A rapidly spreading infection that destroys skin, fat and fascia in the face and neck, usually following dental infection, trauma or surgery. It is life-threatening.
referralThresholdReason: Mortality high without immediate surgery.
urgencyRationale: Life-threatening.
patientAdvice: Go to the emergency department immediately for rapidly spreading painful neck or facial swelling with fever.

name: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
commonName: Autoimmune vasculitis of the nose and airway
description: An autoimmune inflammation of small blood vessels that commonly begins in the nose, sinuses and ears before involving lungs and kidneys. It causes crusting, bloody discharge, nasal septum destruction and hearing loss.
referralThresholdReason: Organ-threatening if delayed.
urgencyRationale: Needs urgent immunosuppression.
patientAdvice: See a doctor promptly for long-standing nasal crusting with bleeding, hearing loss and cough.

name: Recurrent Aphthous Ulcers
description: Recurring small, painful ulcers inside the mouth that heal on their own within one to two weeks. They are common and usually harmless.
referralThresholdReason: Self-limiting.
urgencyRationale: Mostly benign.
patientAdvice: Use salt water rinses. See a doctor if an ulcer lasts more than three weeks.
